hook: Follow 1,000 newborn humans in a wealthy country, 1,000 songbirds that just hatched, and 1,000 oysters that just settled on a reef. Count how many are still alive at each age. The humans mostly make it to old age. The songbirds die at a steady pace all through life. Nearly all the oysters are gone within weeks. Those three patterns are the three survivorship curves.

figure.caption: Type I, II and III survivorship curves, each starting with 1,000 newborns, with survivors on a log scale.

chain.cause: Scientists follow a group of individuals born at the same time and count survivors at each age
chain.effect: they get a survivorship curve: survivors (often on a log scale) plotted against age

chain.cause: Most deaths happen late in life, as with parental care and good protection when young
chain.effect: the curve stays high and then drops steeply at old age: Type I

chain.cause: Deaths happen at a steady rate at every age
chain.effect: the curve falls as a straight line on a log scale: Type II

chain.cause: Most deaths happen very early, as with many unprotected offspring
chain.effect: the curve drops steeply at first, then levels off for the few survivors: Type III

ideas: A survivorship curve shows how many individuals of a group born at the same time are still alive at each age. Survivors are usually plotted on a log scale, starting from 1,000.
Type I: high survival through most of life, with deaths concentrated in old age. Humans in wealthy countries, elephants, many large mammals.
Type II: a steady chance of dying at every age, so the curve is a straight line on a log scale. Many songbirds, lizards, some rodents.
Type III: very many deaths among the young, then high survival for the few that make it. Oysters, most fish, many insects and plants.

misconception.wrong: Survivorship curve and r- or K-selection are the same idea, so a Type III curve means the species is r-selected.
misconception.right: They are related but different. A survivorship curve shows when individuals die; r- and K-selection describe how they reproduce. K-selected species usually have Type I or II curves and r-selected species Type II or III, but the curve alone does not tell you the strategy.

summary: A survivorship curve plots the number of survivors from a group born at the same time against age. Type I curves stay high and drop in old age, Type II curves fall steadily (a straight line on a log scale), and Type III curves drop steeply early in life. Survivorship describes when deaths happen; it is related to, but not the same as, r- and K-selection, which describe how a species reproduces.
